list.listitem: Chronic pancreatitis is a chronic process of inflammation leading to impairment of pancreatic function. In comparison to acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis is generally progressive and may be asymptomatic for a period of time. C
Consider chronic pancreatitis in individuals with chronic abdominal pain, steatorrhea, and weight loss. C
The diagnosis is established by a thorough history, CT, MRI or MRCP, and/or evidence of pancreatic exocrine or endocrine insufficiency. C

Treatment is primarily pain control, initially with medications, and then consideration of endoscopic or surgical procedures if obstructive abnormalities are identified. Early surgery is superior to endoscopic therapy when indicated. B
Prednisone is useful in the treatment of autoimmune pancreatitis, but not other types of chronic pancreatitis. A
Chronic pancreatitis typically progresses as there are no effective methods to stop progression or reverse its course. C
Chronic pancreatitis is a chronic process of inflammation, ductal changes, and fibrosis in the pancreas that can lead to impairment of pancreatic exocrine and endocrine function.
Typical symptoms of chronic pancreatitis include abdominal pain, steatorrhea, and weight loss.

Annual Incidence inthe United States ranges from 5-8 per 100,000 adultsThree studies inform our knowledge of the incidence of chronic pancreatitis, giving a range of 1 to 4 new diagnoses/100,000 persons/year.
An earlier case series from Copenhagen, the United States, and Mexico City reported 4 new episodes/100,000 persons/year.
A recent Japanese study estimates 1 new episode of chronic pancreatitis/100,000 persons/year.
Finally, the incidence rate of chronic pancreatitis in Denmark from 2000 to 2004 was 2.1/100,000 persons/year.
Similarly, estimates of disease prevalence based on these same studies report a range from 12 to 52 per 100,000 persons.
The series from Copenhagen, Mexico City, and the United States reported 13 per 100,000 of population with disease.
In Japan in 2011, the prevalence was 52 per 100,000 persons.
Finally, the prevalence increased in Denmark from 12 per 100,000 person-years in 1985-1989 to 17 per 100,000 person-years in 2000-2004.
Prevalance in the United States up to 42-83 cases per 100 000 adultsWhile acute pancreatitis affects men and women at similar rates, Chronic Pancreatitis affects men more frequently,
African-American patients have a two-to-three-fold prevalence of CP
Intractable or recurrent pain despite medical, endoscopic, and surgical procedures is common. In one cohort study, 115 of 207 patients required surgery for pain relief.
Patients with chronic pancreatitis are at increased risk for pancreatic cancer. A meta-analysis of 6 cohort and 1 case-control studies found a pooled relative risk estimate of 13.3.
Health-related quality of life is reduced, and frequent hospital admissions may be needed to manage pain.
Alcohol abuse: Long-term ingestion of large quantities of alcohol (on average, >5 drinks per day). 5% to 10% of alcoholics develop chronic pancreatitis.
Cigarette smoking: Independent, dose-dependent risk factor in multicenter study of 1000 patients. Associations of smoking with both acute and chronic pancreatitis have been reported.
Hereditary pancreatitis (cationic trypsinogen mutation PRSS1): Autosomal-dominant inheritance pattern. Small subset of cases. Strongly associated with increased risk of pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
Hypercalcemia: May be explained by recurrent acute pancreatitis progressing to chronic pancreatitis.
Tropical pancreatitis: Most common in tropical Africa and much of Asia. Affects children leading to endocrine and exocrine insufficiency in adolescence and frequent death in early adulthood.
Chronic renal failure: Acute and chronic pancreatitis increased in this population. Autopsy study in 78 patients with end-stage renal disease revealed pancreatic fibrosis in 28%.

Idiopathic: Unclear risk factors, may be early or late onset with bimodal age presentation. Early onset: present in first two decades of life with severe abdominal pain. Structural changes, exocrine insufficiency, calcifications occur later in course. Late-onset: occurs in fourth or fifth decades of life, and generally presents with minimal pain though pancreatic insufficiency present at the time of diagnosis.

Auto-immune pancreatitis: Rare. May occur in isolation or in association with other autoimmune diseases. Generally presents with less pain, hypergammaglobulinemia, autoantibodies (ANA<anti-smooth muscle), diffuse enlargement of pancreas on imaging, lack of calcifications and cysts, improvement with steroids.
Five theories have been proposed:

Oxidative—oxidative stress and overactivity of hepatic mixed-function oxidases. These enzymes are initially helpful in detoxification of blood-borne substances, although byproducts of their activity cause reactive molecules that produce oxidative damage to pancreas. This stress leads to inflammation and tissue damage.
Toxic theory with alcohol directly toxic to the acinar cell through change in cellular metabolism leading to fatty degeneration, and cellular necrosis leading to widespread fibrosis.
Stone obstruction causing chronic contraction of the stones leads to ulceration and scarring of ductal epithelial cells.

Necrosis fibrosis theory with acute pancreatitis causes inflammation and scarring in the pancreatic peri-ductular areas. This scarring leads to obstruction of the ductules leading to stasis and then stone formation. Severe obstruction results in atrophy and fibrosis.

Sentinel acute pancreatitis event hypothesis—susceptible individuals may have a triggering factor (alcohol use) leading to activated stellate cells causing chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate, cytokine release leading to collagen deposition.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Summary of TIGAR-O (Toxic-Metabolic, Idiopathic, Genetic, Autoimmune, Recurrent and Severe Acute Pancreatitis, Obstructive) risk factor classification system of risk factors likely associated with development of chronic pancreatitis.
Toxic metabolic: alcoholic, tobacco smoking, hypercalcemia, hyperlipidemia, chronic renal failure.
Recurrent and severe acute pancreatitis: postnecrotic (severe acute pancreatitis), vascular diseases/ischemia, and postradiation exposure
Obstructive: pancreas divisum (controversial), Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (controversial), and duct obstruction (tumors, posttraumatic).

list.listitem: Encourage tobacco cessation. C
Encourage abstaining from alcohol use. C
Consider chronic pancreatitis in individuals with chronic abdominal pain, steatorrhea, and weight loss. C
Order amylase, lipase, a complete metabolic profile, and fecal elastase-1 or serum trypsin. C
Chronic pancreatitis is diagnosed based on imaging (CT being the preferred initial modality) or tests of pancreatic function showing pancreatic insufficiency.C

Even though histologic evidence of fibrosis and tissue loss may be considered the most definitive diagnostic criteria, it is rarely available and may be present in those without CP (such as the very elderly, diabetics, ESRD, tobacco users). C
Consider chronic pancreatitis in individuals with chronic abdominal pain, steatorrhea, and weight loss.

Abdominal pain is usually the dominant feature. Pain is typically epigastric, and often radiates to the back. It may be accompanied by nausea or vomiting, and relieved by sitting upright or leaning forward. Abdominal pain may be more prevalent earlier in the course of the disease, and may initially occur in discrete attacks, and as condition progresses can become continuous.
About 15% of patients are pain-free, although they do have pancreatic exocrine or endocrine dysfunction.
Patients may present with steatorrhea, loose, greasy, foul-smelling stools. Steatorrhea may predate protein deficiencies as lipolytic activity decreases faster than proteolysis.
Steatorrhea is usually a consequence of long standing pancreatitis ( > more than 5 years). Weight loss, especially sarcopenia , is associated with increased mortality risk

Glucose intolerance may be present, though overt diabetes mellitus usually presents later in the disease course. Insulin-requiring DM differs from DM type I as the pancreatic α-cells that produce glucagon are also affected. Patients have an increased risk of treatment-related hypoglycemia.
Clinically significant protein and fat deficiencies related to maldigestion do not occur until over 90% of the glandular function is lost.
Amylase and lipase levels are usually elevated, though may decrease or normalize as the disease progresses.
Liver function tests may show coexistent liver disease of cholestasis due to extrinsic compression of the extrahepatic bile duct.
Elevated ESR or abnormal autoimmune markers such rheumatoid factor, ANA, and anti-smooth muscle antibody titer suggest autoimmune chronic pancreatitis.

If concerned about pancreatic insufficiency, obtain laboratory testing including: serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25[OH]D), serum alpha-tocopherol levels, International normalized ration (INR), prealbumin, B12, Hba1c annually to assess for concomitant pancreatogenic diabetes, serum retinol and retinol-binding protein.
Genetic testing is recommended when there is evidence of a chronic pancreatitis associated disorder, the etiology is unclear, and especially in younger patients.
A panel of metabolic biomarkers (i-Metabolic Signature) was highly accurate at distinguishing ductal pancreatic adenocarcinoma from chronic pancreatitis.

A computed tomography (CT) scan or MRI is recommended by ACG guidelines (2021) as the initial imaging study of choice when evaluating the pancreas. It may be normal early or with minimal change pancreatitis. It is important to perform in all patients to exclude a mass or malignancy. Endoscopic ultrasound is a more invasive alternative.

Characteristic findings on CT or MRI include atrophy of the pancreas, a dilated pancreatic duct, and pancreatic calcifications. These findings are gnomonic of chronic pancreatitis, though can take 5 to 10 years or more to develop.

Secretin enhanced MRI with magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) is recommended by ACG guidelines (2021) as the second-line imaging modality for patients with with equivocal or borderline CT, MRI or endoscopic ultrasound scans. MRI and MRCP can show both parenchymal and ductal findings associated with chronic pancreatitis. Definitive diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis can be made with certainty only by MRI/MRCP when both the main duct and side branches show moderate to marked alterations similar to that seen on a retrograde pancreatogram. Secretin-enhanced MRCP allows for a noninvasive approach to evaluate for pancreatic exocrine function. This method uses IV secretin and observes the T2 intensity changes seen within the pancreatic duct. This allows for better visualization of the pancreatic ducts and side branches.

ERCP is rarely used for diagnosis, though provides the most detailed images of pancreas. Current American Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy guidelines recommend that ERCP be reserved for those patients in whom the diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis has not been established by non-invasive or less invasive studies.

Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) allows for detailed examination of both pancreatic parenchyma and the pancreatic duct. Advantages include ability to detect subtle and severe changes of the pancreatic duct and parenchyma. Limitations include inter- and intra- observer variability, operator dependence. The Rosemont Classification has been proposed as a weighted, standardized method to improve EUS chronic pancreatitis scoring.

At least 5 standard EUS criteria must be met for a diagnosis to be made definitively. Patients with 2 to 5 criteria have an indeterminate diagnosis and should have further evaluation with pancreatic function testing. Compared to secretin pancreatic function test, EUS ≥4 criteria showed a sensitivity of 71 (95% CI, 53%–89%) and specificity of 92% (95% CI, 75%–99%). As most studies of the tests for chronic pancreatitis have a flawed reference standard, the ability to get an actual sensitivity and specificity is difficult.

These EUS criteria demonstrate parenchymal pancreas abnormalities (e.g., (1) hyperechoic foci, (2) hyperechoic strands, (3) lobular contour, and (4) cysts) as well as ductal pancreas abnormalities (e.g., (1) main duct dilation, (2) duct irregular, (3) duct hyperechoic margins, (4) visible side branches, and (5) stones).

A systematic review of 8 studies with 593 patients with chronic pancreatitis found that the pooled sensitivity and specificity of endoscopic ultrasound with fine needle aspiration for evaluation of solid lesions were 65% and 97%, respectively, with LR+ = 20.3 and LR- = 0.36.
DEXA scan should be considered for regular assessment of bone density.

Biochemical tests of pancreatic function are used less commonly than imaging tests. Steatorrhea should be assessed quantitatively. Qualitative evaluation of steatorrhea by Sudan staining of feces should not be done as it is non-specific.
Fecal elastase and serum trypsin are indirect measures of pancreatic function, as they measure the effect of pancreatic enzymes.

Fecal elastase is the indirect test of choice as it is not as cumbersome as the fecal fat excretion. Low levels in the stool (<200 μg/g of stool) are seen in patients with advanced chronic pancreatitis. Serum trypsin levels less than 20 mg/dL are seen in patients with advanced chronic pancreatitis.
Secretin test is a direct test of pancreatic function. It is performed at a few centers and not generally available for most patients.
Further indirect or direct pancreas function testing should only be done if initial imaging and evaluation is equivocal.
In patients presenting with abdominal pain, recurrent pancreatitis, and/or steatorrhea, perform a history and physical focusing on weight loss, diabetes, signs of malabsorption, and jaundice.
Obtain amylase, lipase, a complete metabolic panel, and fecal elastase-1 or serum trypsin.
Initially, obtain imaging with CT scan to rule out a mass. If CT is equivocal, obtain MRCP. If results remain borderline, pursue endoscopic ultrasound.
If no pathology is seen, obtain direct pancreas testing. If any of the imaging is consistent with chronic pancreatitis, proceed with medical management and symptom control.
Assess for complications or alternative diseases such as pancreatic cancer, pseudocyst, bile duct obstruction, duodenal obstruction, and treat if present.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to selecting diagnostic tests.
Treatment of chronic pancreatitis consists primarily of supportive care and pain relief with medications. C
Cessation of alcohol and tobacco use is recommended. C
If treatable complications such as pseudocyst, obstruction, or cancer are found, then more invasive endoscopic or surgical procedures may be appropriate for selected patients.C
Early surgery is superior to endoscopic therapy followed by surgery if needed for patients with obstructive disease. B
Treatment of exocrine insufficiency with pancreatic enzyme replacement should be started in patients after exocrine insufficiency has been diagnosed.A

Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy should be started when exocrine insufficiency is diagnosed. Replacement should begin with 40,000 to 50,000 USP units of lipase with each meal and half that amount with snacks. In one study, a new formulation of 72,000 lipase units per main meal and 36,000 lipase units per snack improved fat absorption and improved clinical symptoms.
The goal of treatment is to avoid complications of malnutrition and not to treat pain.
Pain management with analgesics is generally required. Limiting narcotics and using the lowest potency when starting is important, with a goal of pain reduction, not elimination.

As with other chronic pain, tricyclic antidepressants, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, and gabapentoids can be used. Only pregabalin has been studied in an RCT for chronic pancreatitis. Pregabalin up to 300 mg twice daily reduced pain compared to those given placebo, and those given pregabalin were able to reduce their opioid dose. The study did find more adverse side effects of “feeling of being drunk or lightheaded” in the intervention group. Furthermore, an extensive placebo response (24%) was seen in this study.
A small double-blind crossover study looking at the use of octreotide did not find any improvement in pain.

Pancreatic enzyme supplements may suppress pancreatic exocrine secretion to relieve pain in some patients. Study results have been mixed, perhaps given differences in enzyme preparations used, endpoints measured and high placebo response rates. A Cochrane review of 10 studies was unable to pool the results of the studies, nor make a definitive conclusion on their use. Two positive controlled trials suggest patients with less advanced disease (without involvement of large ducts and without steatorrhea), women, and those with idiopathic chronic pancreatitis benefit the most.

Antioxidant therapy has yielded mixed results in two large randomized trials but is recommended by ACG guidelines (2021). The ANTICIPATE study did not find pain control improvement in patients with chronic pancreatitis of predominantly alcoholic etiology. One study found a reduction in pain and levels of oxidative stress, though their patient population was younger with predominantly idiopathic pancreatitis. The decreased micronutrient intake (vitamin E, riboflavin, magnesium, copper) of patients due to diet modifications related to pain may contribute to increased oxidative stress. A Cochrane review from 2014 suggests slight pain reduction with antioxidants, though adverse effects such as headache and GI complaints occurred in 16% of participants. Outcomes such as use of analgesics, exacerbation of pancreatitis, and quality of life were rarely reported.

Autoimmune pancreatitis can be treated with corticosteroids, though relapses may occur. High-dose corticosteroid therapy with prednisone dosing of approximately 30–40 mg/day results in more rapid, consistent induction of disease remission.
Endoscopic therapy to remove stones or address stricture in the main pancreatic duct may be helpful in selected patients. Ductal abnormalities may not correlate with symptoms.

ACT guidelines (2021) recommend surgery over futher endoscopic therapy for treatment of obstructive disease if initial endoscopic approaches have been unsuccessful. This was consistent with findings of the Dutch ESCAPE trial that randomized 88 patients to early surgery or endoscopic therapy followed by later surgery if needed. Those in the early surgery group had a lower pain score and a trend toward a greater likelihood of partial or complete pain relief (58% vs 39%, p = .10). Complications, hospitalizations and other outcomes were similar between groups. Early surgery was also more cost-effective. 8 year follow up of ESCAPE trial reaffirmed long-term outcomes and notably patients who progressed from endoscopy to surgery had worse outcomes compared to patients undergoing early surgery.

A retrospective analysis of 1000 patients treated with a variety of endoscopic techniques found 65% success in an intention-to-treat analysis for the outcome of pain reduction. After a mean period of 4.9 years, 69% of patients with endotherapy were pain-free. Of the study patients, 25% ended up having an additional procedure or surgery for refractory pain.

Large stones or impacted stones usually require extracorporeal shock wave lithrotripsy (ESWL). One randomized control study found no significance in pain relief between those who underwent ESWL followed by ERCP versus those who only had ESWL. Breaking up the stones may be sufficient to improve ductal drainage and relieve pain.

Surgery is an option for patients who have not responded to medical or endoscopic therapy; those with local complications such as duodenal or biliary obstruction; concern for malignancy. Dite compared endoscopic to surgical therapies for pain. One year after intervention pain relief was equivalent between the two groups. After 5 years, 34% of patients in surgery group and 15% of endoscopy group still had complete pain relief. Partial relief was equivalent between the two groups (approximately 50%).

Surgical intervention trials included patients with ductal anatomies amenable to endoscopic or surgical therapies; primarily those with a dilated pancreatic duct or an obstructing stone or stricture. In this population, surgery seems to be somewhat more effective and durable than endoscopic therapy. Small trials did not provide sufficient power to detect small differences in outcomes.
Endoscopic ultrasound-guided celiac plexus neurolysis provides some pain relief in chronic pancreatitis, though response is not as long-acting or effective as for pancreatic cancer.
Diet low in fat and small in quantity (fat limitation to 50 g/day) is thought to avoid excessive stimulation of the pancreas, though this has never been evaluated in a clinical trial.
Refer to specialist for invasive procedures especially those with complicated anatomy.
Cessation of alcohol use in patients who drink alcohol is strongly recommended.
Smoking cessation is also strongly recommended.

A study randomized 106 patients with chronic pancreatitis to extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy (ESWL) or sham ESWL. Those receiving ESWL had a 0.7 greater improvement on a 10 point visual pain scale, which is of borderline clinical significance.
Chronic pancreatitis is a difficult to manage condition with an emphasis on symptom control. There is no documented increase in mortality related to the disease itself. C
For patients with early disease but with persistent abdominal pain, repeated imaging may be required until one is able to make the radiographic diagnosis. C
Patients should be followed to evaluate for pancreatic insufficiency, with treatment with pancreatic enzymes started if insufficiency develops. C
A higher Hospital Frailty Risk Score predicts a greater likelihood of mortality and hospitalization in patients with chronic pancreatitis.
